claims.text: A post-sintering thermal treatment can invert a refractory HEA microstructure from a continuous ordered phase to a continuous disordered BCC matrix containing discrete ordered precipitates.
The microstructural inversion will synergistically improve yield strength, ductility, Young's modulus, and fracture resistance relative to conventional processing.
A powder-metallurgy refractory HEA can initially contain a predominantly continuous brittle ordered B2 phase and secondary phases.
The continuous ordered phase provides high strength while limiting ductility and fracture resistance.
Solutionizing at approximately 1400 °C for 20 minutes followed by annealing at approximately 600 °C for 120 hours is a suitable inversion treatment.
The solutionizing step dissolves the continuous brittle ordered phase.
Controlled low-temperature annealing re-precipitates the dissolved components as fine, discrete ordered particles.
The resulting precipitates are approximately 50 nm in size.
A continuous disordered BCC matrix optimizes dislocation mobility and thereby improves ductility.
A continuous disordered BCC matrix improves fracture resistance.
Discrete ordered precipitates provide precipitation strengthening that preserves or enhances yield strength.
The inverted microstructure provides solid-solution strengthening.
The inverted microstructure maintains a robust or slightly improved Young's modulus.
The treated HEA will achieve a yield strength of approximately 1300–1400 MPa.
The treated HEA will exhibit a fracture strain exceeding 25%.
The treated HEA will have enhanced fracture resistance, evidenced by reduced crack initiation and propagation.
Refractory HEAs processed without this intervention typically have a continuous brittle ordered phase, high strength, poor ductility, and limited fracture resistance.
Phase inversion is enabled by elemental partitioning or solubility differences in systems such as NbTaTiV or Al0.5NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr.
The approach works best when the starting microstructure is homogeneous and the alloy chemistry supports dissolution and re-precipitation.
Insufficient segregation or solubility differences, or substantial deviations in temperature, holding time, or cooling rate, can prevent inversion and the expected property improvements.
